in_context.text: Paul has just warned that some will turn from the faith and teach that people must not marry and must avoid certain foods (4:1-3). He answers that everything God made is good when received with thanks (4:4-5). In verse 6 he tells Timothy that reminding the believers of these truths is what makes him a good servant of Christ.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in Paul's name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: "The brethren," meaning the believers in the church, who need to be reminded of the truth over against the false teaching.

what.text: Paul promises that if Timothy sets these truths before the believers, he will be a good servant of Jesus Christ. Timothy himself is fed by the words of the faith and the good teaching he has closely followed.

events.text: The verse gives instruction rather than describing an event. It is set while Timothy led the church in Ephesus after Paul went on to Macedonia.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where Paul wrote from is not stated, though it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul is coaching a young leader on how to meet false teaching. The answer is to keep reminding the church of sound truth and to stay fed on it himself.

big_picture.text: The letter teaches that sound teaching and godly living belong together. This verse opens a section where Timothy is to devote himself to reading, teaching, and his own life, so that he saves himself and his hearers.

for_readers.text: Good Christian service here is not novelty but faithful reminding of truth one has already learned. Other passages also stress remembrance and continuing in what was learned.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to lay something before someone or suggest it. It points to setting truth before the believers, not issuing harsh orders.
Diakonos means a servant or attendant in general. Here "servant of Christ" describes Timothy's role, not a formal church title.
This word means to be trained up or nurtured. It pictures the leader being continually fed by the words of the faith before feeding others.
The KJV "attained" translates a word meaning to follow closely as a standard of conduct. Timothy has not merely reached the teaching; he has been living by it.

takeaway.text: A good servant of Christ keeps reminding God's people of the truth, especially when error spreads. He can only do that if he keeps feeding on that truth himself.
